objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain, demonstrate from the right seat and teach a constant airspeed climb solely by reference to instruments, straight and turning, with a level-off inside the CFI standard, and you can spot and fix the instrument climb errors learners make.
why: Private pilot applicants must get flight training in constant airspeed climbs solely by reference to instruments [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109]], and you will be the one giving it. A VFR pilot with no instrument training, or with eroded skills, loses control in about 10 minutes once forced onto the instruments [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. A climb on instruments changes pitch, power and airspeed at once, and the IFH lists a slow cross-check during climb entries as a common error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

prereading.label: IFH 7-24 to 7-25

prereading.label: IFH 7-44 to 7-51

prereading.label: PHAK 8-8 to 8-19

warmup: Think first: your learner, under the hood, raises the nose for a climb and adds power. Ten seconds later the airspeed is 8 knots slow, the VSI shows 900 fpm and the heading has drifted 10 degrees left. Which one instrument would you ask them to look at first, what would you say, and which of these three problems would you leave for later?

key_terms.def: Controlling the airplane's position in space by instruments instead of outside references [[23:134|IFH 6-1]].
Set attitude and power on the control instruments, trim, cross-check the performance instruments, then adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]].
Instruments grouped by what they control (pitch, bank, power, trim); the primary one gives the most pertinent information for that phase [[23:137|IFH 6-4]] [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].
The instrument that gives the most pertinent information for a particular maneuver, usually the one to hold at a constant indication [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].
The continuous and logical observation of instruments for attitude and performance information; also called scanning [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Understanding how each instrument works, then applying that to the airplane, the maneuver and the conditions to read its attitude [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
The width of the miniature aircraft wings and center dot on the attitude indicator, about 2 degrees of pitch [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].
The delay before the VSI shows a stable rate after a pitch change, about 6 to 9 seconds; rough control makes it longer [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]].
A climb at a set climb power in which pitch holds one airspeed; once stable the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Starting the level-off before the target altitude, about 10 percent of the vertical speed, because the airplane keeps climbing through the transition [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].
Staring at a single instrument; it usually has a reason but gives poor results [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].
Leaving an instrument out of the cross-check, often from not expecting its indications to change after an attitude change [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

chunks.title: Where this Task fits and what the examiner sees

body.p: A constant airspeed climb holds one climb airspeed at a set climb power. For a given power and load there is one attitude that gives the most efficient climb; the POH/AFM gives the airspeed and climb power. Entry technique depends on the airspeed at entry and on the type of climb, constant airspeed or constant rate [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The IFH maneuvers assume a single-engine airplane with retractable gear and flaps, so adapt them to your trainer [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

Private pilot applicants need 3 hours of flight training solely by reference to instruments, and constant airspeed climbs are on the list [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109]]. This lesson builds on AI.XI.A (instrument straight-and-level flight), which covers the basics of attitude instrument flying, the cross-check and the safety pilot. Here we stay on what changes in the climb. Visual climbs are in AI.VIII.C.

Function and operation, in one line: the IFH teaches two methods that use the same instruments and control responses. Control and performance sets attitude and power on the control instruments and checks the performance instruments; primary and supporting groups the instruments by pitch, bank and power [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]. Use the one your learner learned in AI.XI.A and name the instruments the same way every flight.

callout.text: CFI ACS AI.XI.B.S3: "Level off at the assigned altitude and maintain altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, and airspeed ±10 knots." The Private ACS (PA.VIII.B.S3) allows ±200 feet and ±20°, with the same ±10 knots. Area XI Note: "The evaluator must select at least one Task from this Area of Operation." (FAA-S-ACS-25; FAA-S-ACS-6)

check.q: Your private learner says the checkride only needs ±200 feet, so why should they aim for zero error? What do you tell them?
check.a: Unless zero error is the goal, a pilot tolerates larger and larger deviations; a 1° error takes far less effort to fix than a 20° one [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]. Deviations are expected but not accepted [[23:205|IFH 7-44]].

body.p: Indication of the aircraft attitude: the attitude indicator is the only instrument that shows the actual flight attitude both instantly and directly; it is the basic attitude reference and should always be used when available [[23:140|IFH 6-7]] [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. Its picture matches the airplane against the real horizon, including the climbing turns:

bullets: Pitch is read in bar widths. The miniature wings and dot equal about 2° of pitch [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. The climb picture varies with the airplane type [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Bank: use the banking scale only for how much bank; read the direction of bank from the miniature aircraft against the horizon bar, because some scales move the opposite way [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]].

The miniature aircraft is set level at cruise in level flight and should not be moved for flight at other speeds, so the instrument shows a true picture in every maneuver [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]. In the climb it sits above the horizon bar; do not let a learner "re-zero" it there.

Pitch is also read from the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI; bank from the heading indicator and turn coordinator [[23:147|IFH 6-14]]. At constant power, a falling airspeed means the pitch has moved higher; a rising one means it has lowered [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

body.p: Instrument interpretation starts here. Attitude plus power equals performance: the same picture gives very different results in different airplanes, so the learner must learn what to expect from this airplane in this maneuver [[23:146|IFH 6-13]] [[23:147|IFH 6-14]].

callout.text: Before the hood goes on, fly the climb visually and have the learner compare the nose on the natural horizon with the attitude indicator. The IFH suggests the instructor demonstrate pitch changes this way, comparing the instrument with the airplane's position on the horizon [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].

check.q: Your learner sees the bank pointer at the top of the attitude indicator move left and calls a left bank. What do you teach?
check.a: Use the scale only for the amount of bank. Read the direction from the miniature aircraft against the horizon bar, since some scales move opposite to the bank [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]].

chunks.title: Function and operation of each instrument in the climb

body.p: Function and operation: the control instruments (attitude indicator and power gauges) show attitude and power directly; the performance instruments (altimeter, airspeed, VSI) show what the airplane is actually doing [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]. Each one has a different job as the climb develops:

head: Instrument
How it works
Its job in a constant airspeed climb
rows: Attitude indicator
A gyro rigid in space; the airplane rotates around it [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. Pneumatic or electric powered [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
Set the climb pitch on entry; supporting pitch and bank once stable [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:176|IFH 7-15]]
Airspeed indicator
Differential pressure gauge: pitot pressure against static pressure [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]
Primary for pitch once the climb is stable [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Vertical speed indicator
Trend first (direction of needle movement), then a stabilized rate [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]
Supporting pitch; should trend up at once, then stop at a rate that fits the airspeed and attitude [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Altimeter
Aneroid capsules measure outside pressure [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Tells you when to start the level-off; primary for pitch during the level-off [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Heading indicator
Gyro that is not north seeking; set it to the compass [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Primary for bank in the straight climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Turn coordinator
Canted gyro: shows roll rate, then rate of turn; the ball shows coordination [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]
Supporting bank straight ahead; primary for bank in an established standard-rate turn [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
Tachometer or manifold pressure
Power indicators, not affected by turbulence, trim or stray control pressure [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]
Primary for power: confirms climb power is held [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]

body.p: A normally aspirated engine loses power as it climbs: RPM falls with a fixed-pitch propeller and manifold pressure falls with a controllable one, so the pilot checks the engine instruments to keep climb power set [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

check.q: Your learner says the VSI is the best pitch instrument in the climb because it moves first. What do you add?
check.a: It shows the trend first, but the stable rate lags about 6 to 9 seconds [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]. In a constant airspeed climb the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch once stable, and the VSI supports [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

chunks.title: Instrument limitations and potential errors in a climb

body.p: Instrument limitations and potential errors matter more in a climb, because pitch, power and airspeed all change at once. Teach each one with what the learner will actually see:

head: Instrument
Limitation or error
What it looks like in the climb
rows: VSI
Lag of about 6 to 9 seconds before the rate is stable [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]. A large, abrupt pitch change gives erratic movement and even a reverse indication [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
An abrupt entry shows a dip or a wild swing, and a learner who chases it overcontrols
VSI out of calibration
May show a climb or descent in level flight; allow for that error, or use the reading as the zero [[23:166|IFH 7-5]] [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]
The climb rate reads high or low by the same amount
Airspeed indicator
No real lag in the instrument; the delay is the airplane slowing down [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Speed decays smoothly for some seconds after the pitch change; that is the airplane, not the gauge
Attitude indicator

Slight nose-up in rapid acceleration, nose-down in rapid deceleration, small errors after a 180° turn; they correct within about a minute of straight-and-level flight [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. Pitch and bank limits depend on the model; past them some peg or tumble [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]
A small false pitch after a quick level-off and acceleration to cruise
Heading indicator
Drifts; check it against the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
A long climb can end on the "right" heading that is actually off
Magnetic compass
Affected by climbing, power changes and airspeed adjustments; leads and lags in turns [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]
On east or west headings, the speed change at entry and level-off swings the card [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Vacuum-driven gyros
Low suction makes the attitude and heading indicators unreliable [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]
Check the suction gauge in the cross-check, not just before takeoff

bullets: Static system blocked: the altimeter freezes and the VSI reads zero, and the airspeed reads lower than actual above the altitude where it blocked [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. In a climb this looks like "no climb" with climb power and a nose-up picture.
Pitot tube and drain hole blocked: the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter, reading higher as the airplane climbs [[23:98|IFH 5-3]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

callout.text: A learner who trusts one failed instrument can "fix" the airplane into a stall or a dive (application). Before any control input, cross-check all the relevant instruments [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

check.q: Climb power is set, the attitude indicator shows the normal climb picture, but the altimeter has not moved for a minute and the VSI sits on zero. Is the airplane level?
check.a: Probably not. That pattern fits a blocked static system: the altimeter freezes and the VSI reads zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. Trust the attitude and power, and use the alternate static source if installed [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

chunks.title: Primary and supporting instruments, and the climb cross-check

body.p: Proper instrument cross-check techniques: no single method is required. Use the instruments that give the best information for the phase you are in; those are usually the ones held at a constant indication, and the others help keep them there [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. In the selected radial cross-check the pilot spends 80 to 90 percent of the time on the attitude indicator, and the eyes travel to every other instrument by way of it [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].
Through the climb, the instrument in charge changes:

head: Phase
Pitch
Bank
Power
rows: Entry (Fig 7-25)
Attitude indicator and VSI supporting; no primary pitch is labeled
Heading indicator primary
Power gauge primary
Stable climb (Fig 7-26)
Airspeed indicator primary
Heading indicator primary
Tachometer or manifold pressure primary
Level-off to cruise (Fig 7-29)
Altimeter primary
Heading indicator primary
Airspeed indicator primary as it nears the desired value

body.p: From [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:176|IFH 7-15]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. The entry and the stable climb look like this:

Instrument interpretation ties it together. A pilot sees low airspeed, decides the nose is high, and pushes, without noticing that low power is the cause; the fix is a faster cross-check of every relevant instrument before any control input [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. In the climb that means a glance at the tachometer before a pitch change. Cross-check both airspeed and vertical speed before adjusting pitch or power [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].
Speed the cross-check up whenever pitch, power or airspeed are changing, and especially during climb entries; not doing so is a listed climb error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

On a primary flight display the logic is the same: raise the yellow chevron to the planned pitch, set climb power, and once stable the airspeed tape is primary for pitch, the heading indicator for bank and the tachometer or manifold pressure for power [[23:207|IFH 7-46]] [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

check.q: Your learner asks why the attitude indicator is "only supporting" in the stable climb when they look at it most. What do you answer?
check.a: Primary means the instrument with the most pertinent information for the phase, the one held constant [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]; in the stable climb that is the airspeed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The attitude indicator is still the basic reference and the hub of the cross-check [[23:143|IFH 6-10]] [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

chunks.title: Entering the climb: pitch, power, coordination and trim

body.p: From cruise airspeed, on an assigned heading [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]:

bullets: Raise the miniature aircraft to the approximate nose-high picture for the climb speed, with light back pressure. The pressures change as the airplane slows.
Power: advance to climb power with the pitch change, or after the pitch is set and the airspeed nears climb speed. The IFH allows both.
Watch the VSI: a smooth entry shows an immediate upward trend, then the needle slows and stops at a rate that fits the airspeed and attitude.
Hold the heading: the heading indicator stays primary for bank.

body.p: From climb airspeed: first slow to climb speed in straight-and-level flight, then raise the pitch and add climb power at the same time. Entries on partial panel are easier and more accurate from climb speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. On the PFD the IFH shows why the timing matters: power added after the pitch change lets the airspeed drop from the extra drag; power added first makes it rise from the excess thrust [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

Control application solely by reference to instruments: pitch changes on instruments are much smaller than visual ones [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]. A tight grip makes control pressure hard to feel; make small, smooth changes with positive pressure, and momentarily release pressure when tense, since a trimmed airplane holds its attitude [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]. More power makes a single-engine airplane yaw and roll left unless aileron and rudder are applied, so the cross-check must speed up [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Keep the ball centered: step on the ball [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]].

Trimming the aircraft: hold the new attitude with control pressure, then trim so the airplane keeps it with the controls released; center the ball with rudder trim if installed [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Using trim alone to change attitude leads to erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. The airplane is trimmed for an airspeed, not a pitch attitude [[23:206|IFH 7-45]], so every airspeed change in the entry needs more trim [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. Trim often and in small amounts [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

callout.text: Establish, trim, cross-check, adjust: the IFH four-step process for any attitude change [[23:152|IFH 6-19]]. Say it out loud on every entry.

check.q: Your learner sets the climb attitude by rolling in nose-up trim. What does the IFH say about that?
check.a: Using trim alone to change attitude leads to erratic control. Set the attitude with control pressure, then trim to relieve it [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

chunks.title: Holding the climb, straight and in turns

body.p: Once the climb is stable, hold the airspeed with small pitch changes and let the rate be what it is. If the attitude is right for the power, the airspeed settles on the target; if it is low or high, make an appropriately small pitch correction [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Use corrections of no more than half a bar width at a time on the attitude indicator [[23:138|IFH 6-5]].

Do not mix this up with a constant-rate climb, where the VSI becomes primary for pitch and the airspeed primary for power once the rate settles [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Learners who know only the VSI tend to chase it [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. The ACS Task here is constant airspeed.

Climbing turns: combine the straight-climb technique with the turn technique, allow for the lift and power changes, and speed up the cross-check to cover bank as well as pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. The IFH spells out the turn technique only for a level standard-rate turn. Here is what carries over:

bullets: Bank for a standard-rate turn is about 15 percent of true airspeed: divide by 10 and add half the result [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

Bank carries over: roll in on the attitude indicator, then use the turn coordinator as primary for bank and the attitude indicator as supporting; note the bank angle that gives standard rate [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

Pitch changes: as the bank increases the vertical lift drops, and in the level turn the IFH has you check the altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator for pitch [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. With climb power fixed, the same pitch and airspeed cannot both be held in a bank, so the airplane climbs a little more shallowly [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Keep holding the climb airspeed with pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] (application).
Trim off the pressures once the bank is set, and check the ball throughout, especially if pressures are held instead of trimmed [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

Roll out at the same rate as the roll-in, leading the heading by half the bank angle; the attitude indicator is primary for bank during the roll-out and the heading indicator once level [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
On a 90° turn at standard rate, leave the heading indicator out of the cross-check for about 20 seconds; staring at it is fixation [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

body.p: Figure 7-33 is a level standard-rate turn at constant airspeed: the altimeter is primary for pitch and the airspeed for power. The IFH has no instrument figure for a climbing turn. Only the bank roles carry over; in the climbing turn climb power stays fixed and pitch holds the airspeed (application of [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]).

check.q: Which parts of the IFH level standard-rate turn carry over to a climbing turn, and which do not?
check.a: Bank carries over: roll in on the attitude indicator, then the turn coordinator is primary for bank [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Pitch does not: Figure 7-33 makes the altimeter primary for pitch in a level turn [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; in a climbing turn at climb power, pitch holds the climb airspeed (application of [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]).

chunks.title: Leveling off at the assigned altitude

body.p: Start before the altitude. The airplane keeps climbing at a decreasing rate through the transition, so lead by about 10 percent of the vertical speed: 500 fpm, 50 feet; 1,000 fpm, 100 feet [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].
To level off at cruise airspeed [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]:

bullets: Apply smooth, steady forward pressure toward the level attitude for the speed desired.
As the attitude indicator shows the change, the VSI moves slowly toward zero, the altimeter slows, and the airspeed starts to build.
Keep climb power while the airplane accelerates; expect steady pitch and torque corrections as the speed rises.
Reduce to cruise power as the airspeed approaches cruise. The lead depends on how fast the airplane accelerates.

body.p: To level off and stay at climb airspeed: lower the nose to the level attitude for that airspeed and reduce power at the same time; if the power comes off in proportion to the pitch change, the airspeed stays constant [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

Trimming the aircraft again: trim off the pressures and go back to the straight-and-level cross-check. After the first level-off from a climb, check that the attitude indicator shows level at normal cruise and adjust the miniature aircraft if needed [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Keep an accelerated cross-check until fully established in level flight [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

head: After level-off
CFI standard (AI.XI.B.S3)
Private standard (PA.VIII.B.S3)
rows: Altitude
±100 feet
±200 feet
Heading
Airspeed
±10 knots
±10 knots

body.p: Holding it: for altitude errors under 100 feet use a half bar width correction, over 100 feet start with a full bar width [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Aim for a vertical speed about double the error: 100 feet off, about 200 fpm back [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

callout.text: An abrupt change from climb to level flight can cause the inversion illusion, a feeling of tumbling backward; the disoriented pilot may push abruptly nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. A smooth level-off at the right lead is the prevention.

check.q: Your learner is climbing at 650 fpm to 7,000 feet and wants to level off at cruise. At what altitude does the level-off start, and when does power come back?
check.a: About 6,935 feet (10 percent of 650 is 65 feet). Climb power stays in until the airspeed nears cruise, then cruise power [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

body.p: Fixation and omission are the two cross-check faults the ACS names. The IFH adds a third, emphasis on a single instrument [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]:

head: Fault
What it is
Climb example
rows: Fixation
Staring at one instrument; tension creeps into the controls and causes errors elsewhere [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Staring at the airspeed while the heading drifts; gazing at the manifold pressure gauge during a power change, though the airplane will not decelerate any faster [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Omission
Leaving an instrument out, often from not expecting it to change after an attitude change [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Leveling off on the attitude indicator alone and never checking the heading indicator [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Emphasis
Relying on the instrument that is easiest to understand, even when it is wrong or not enough [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Holding the level-off on the attitude indicator alone; it cannot give precise altitude without the altimeter [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]

body.p: The AIH says beginning instrument pilots characteristically fixate on particular instruments while other parts of their performance deteriorate. Fixation is often a sign that the task has not had enough practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. To spot it, glance at the learner's eyes: a long look at one instrument suggests fixation; a gaze that never reaches the engine instruments suggests inattention. Looking in the same direction is not the same as seeing, so the technique has limits [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

Instrument interpretation: in level flight, when the airspeed is off, check the altimeter before deciding a power change is needed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. The climb version: check the power gauge before blaming pitch. Low airspeed in the climb with climb power set means pitch; low airspeed with low power means power [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness, or disorientation all show up in the climb:

bullets: Distractions: a pilot cannot look at two things at once; switching attention risks forgetting the deferred task [[25:80|AIH 3-29]] [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Make sure each task is done well in isolation before combining them [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].
Task prioritization: attend to the most important tasks first; keep the pitch attitude constant and more time is left for cross-check and interpretation [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

Loss of situational awareness: a learner absorbed in one gauge stops tracking altitude, heading and power (application). The AIH lists realistic distractions to train for this, including a 200-foot climb and level-off [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].
Disorientation: a head movement in a different plane during a turn can cause the coriolis illusion. Cross-check with minimal head movement and pick up dropped items carefully [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

check.q: Under the hood your learner's eyes have been on the VSI for 15 seconds during a climbing turn. What is likely happening to the rest of the flight, and what is the AIH's explanation?
check.a: Fixation: one item is controlled while others deteriorate, such as bank and airspeed [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. It often means the task needs more practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

chunks.title: Instrument flying hazards and getting help

body.p: Instrument flying hazards, including the six the ACS lists, and how each shows up in a climb:

head: Hazard
In the climb
What you teach
rows: Failure to maintain VFR
A pilot who cannot keep attitude by the natural horizon is in IMC for practical purposes, whatever the weather report says [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]
Accept it as a genuine emergency; integrated or hood training does not prepare a pilot for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Spatial disorientation

An abrupt climb-to-level change can feel like tumbling backward; a rapid acceleration can feel nose-up and invite a push [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Uncoordinated climbing turns send misleading signals [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]
Smooth level-offs, coordinated turns, and belief in the instruments over the senses [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]
Loss of control
Untrained or rusty pilots lose control in about 10 minutes on instruments [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Combined maneuvers such as climbing turns compound the problems [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]
For a pilot caught in IMC: keep the wings level, raise the nose no more than one bar width, add power and accept whatever speed results [[24:367|AFH 18-18]] [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]
Fatigue
Fatigue degrades attention, concentration and coordination [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]; fatigue or illness makes disorientation sensations worse [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]
Skill fatigue narrows attention to the center of vision: the same shape as fixation [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]
Stress
Chronic stress makes performance fall off sharply [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]
Relax, use fingertip pressure, "control with the eyes and the brain" [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]
Emergency off airport landings
A precautionary landing, while further flight is still possible, is generally less hazardous than a forced one [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]
A non-instrument-rated pilot trapped by weather who does not consider one accepts an extremely hazardous alternative [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]

body.p: The IFH lists in-flight demonstrations of disorientation. Two fit this Task: climbing while accelerating (eyes closed, the instructor accelerates level, and the usual feeling is a climb) and climbing while turning (a slow, coordinated turn of about 1.5 G feels like a climb) [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Do not attempt them at low altitude or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

When to seek assistance or declare an emergency in a deteriorating situation: an aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything else affecting safety. That is the time to ask for help, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. A non-instrument-rated pilot who cannot continue in VFR conditions should tell the controller, say there is no instrument rating, and declare distress [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]; squawk 7700 to alert radar [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]. If a controller's urgency is rushing the pilot into a maneuver, ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

callout.text: The AFH emergency climb (one bar width, any speed) is a survival technique for an untrained pilot; the constant airspeed climb is the trained skill. Teach both, and say which one you are teaching [[24:369|AFH 18-20]] [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

check.q: Your learner asks why you teach a precise climb when the AFH says a pilot caught in cloud should just raise the nose one bar width. What do you say?
check.a: The AFH climb is a survival technique for an untrained pilot: no more than one bar width, add power, accept the speed [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. The constant airspeed climb is the trained skill the ACS tests [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

body.p: Collision hazards rise in hood work. When weather permits, every pilot must keep watch to see and avoid other aircraft, IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat with adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. The safety pilot's duties are in AI.XI.A.

bullets: Instructors and safety pilots tend to "look inside" excessively during simulated instrument flight; guard against preoccupation with the lesson [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

The climb attitude blocks the view ahead. In a climb a pilot can adjust the pitch attitude to see over the nose [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]; the learner under the hood cannot look, so you must (application).
A flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the midair collisions in the study the AIH cites [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
Clear the area before the climb entry, as before any training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

body.p: On the practical test, brief with the examiner when and how the view-limiting device goes on and comes off. It must block the applicant's outside view but not the evaluator's ability to see and avoid traffic (FAA-S-ACS-25, Equipment Requirements and Limitations). Use the same brief with your learners.

check.q: Before the first climb entry in the practice area, what do you do, and what statistic backs it up?
check.a: Clear the area, as before any training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. In the midair collision study the AIH cites, a flight instructor was aboard in 37 percent of the accidents [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

body.p: On the ground, brief the objective, the completion standard and the safety items [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]: the climb speed and climb power for your airplane [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], the climb picture in bar widths, who is primary in each phase, the 10 percent lead, and the hood and traffic plan.

head: Step
For instrument climbs
rows: Build the blocks

Instrument references start the first time climbs are introduced visually [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Airspeed changes in straight-and-level flight build all three instrument skills first [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. Then straight climbs from climb speed, where the speed reduction is done first and only pitch and power change together [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], then from cruise, then climbing turns and level-offs to assigned altitudes.
Demonstrate and explain

From the right seat, name the power setting and attitude as you fly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Show an overcontrolled correction and then the slower, smoother one, as the IFH suggests for pitch [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].
Learner practice

Have the learner say "attitude, power, trim, cross-check" and name the primary instrument at each phase. Watch their eyes for fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Be ready to take control, especially on the first attempts [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Add load
Once the climb is consistent, add distractions such as reading the OAT or a 200-foot altitude change [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], then climbing turns to headings.
Evaluate
Level-offs to assigned altitudes against the standard you briefed.

bullets: Teach the fingertip grip early: a tight grip hides control pressures [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].
Ask "What is primary for pitch right now?" at entry, in the stable climb and at the level-off. The answer changes three times [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
Tie it to real use: a climb on a vector or out of a lowering ceiling. Make sure learners understand that hood training does not prepare them for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: If the learner is consistently late with pitch on entries, stop, go back to straight-and-level, and practice the smaller change first; the IFH gives this advice for steep turns and it fits any entry [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

check.q: Your learner recites "attitude, power, trim, cross-check" but trims only after several scans. What order does the IFH give?
check.a: Establish the attitude and power, trim, cross-check, then adjust [[23:152|IFH 6-19]]. The airplane is trimmed by first holding the attitude with pressure, then trimming that pressure off [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

body.p: The rows below are the IFH lists for straight climbs (analog and PFD) and for turns [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Overcontrolling pitch on climb entry
Large pitch swings; VSI more than 200 fpm past the target [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Small, smooth pressures; wait for the result before adding more [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Not speeding up the cross-check on entry
Heading or bank errors build while the pitch is changing
Faster cross-check whenever pitch or power changes [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Not holding the new pitch attitude
Nose creeps up or sags as the speed decays
Keep cross-checking, readjust pressure, trim [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Not trimming off pressures
Pitch wanders when the learner is distracted
Trim after every change [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]
Not knowing the power settings
Repeated power corrections, slow climbs
Learn the pitch and power numbers for the airplane [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Not cross-checking airspeed and VSI together
A pitch fix for a power problem, or the reverse
Check both before changing either [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Chasing the VSI
Pitch oscillates with the needle
Use the attitude indicator as the control instrument; cross-check the other pitch instruments [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]
No level-off lead
Altitude overshoot
Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
Poor pitch and power coordination on a slow-speed level-off
Airspeed falls or rises at the new altitude
Reduce power in proportion to the pitch change [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
Slow cross-check after level-off
Drift right after a good level-off
Accelerated cross-check until established in level flight [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Turns: pitch not changed as the vertical lift changes
In a level turn, altitude lost on entry or gained on roll-out [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; in a climbing turn, expect airspeed swings instead (application)
Adjust pitch as the bank goes in and as it comes out [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Turns: preoccupied with bank on entry
Pitch errors while rolling in
Check the pitch instruments as the bank pressures start [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]

body.p: Analyze and correct: on the checkride the examiner may fly as your learner and make one of these errors. Name what you see, give the cause, demonstrate the fix, then let the "learner" try again; this matches the AIH reteaching sequence [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: The examiner, as your learner, enters the climb with large pitch swings and the VSI 300 fpm past the planned rate. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Overcontrolling pitch on climb entry: more than 200 fpm past the desired rate shows overcontrolling [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]. Use small, smooth pressures and check the result before adding more [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

f1.caption: Figure 8-24. Attitude representation by the attitude indicator corresponds to the relation of the aircraft to the real horizon.
f1.alt: Nine panels, each with an attitude indicator above a small airplane. Top row: climbing left bank, straight climb, climbing right bank, with the horizon line below the miniature aircraft. Middle row: level left bank, a large labeled attitude indicator (pointer, bank scale marked 10, 20, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees, artificial horizon, adjustment knob), level right bank. Bottom row: descending left bank, straight descent, descending right bank.

f2.caption: Figure 7-25. Climb entry for constant airspeed climb.
f2.alt: Six-pack panel with manifold pressure and RPM gauges during the climb entry. Labels: attitude indicator supporting pitch and bank, power gauges primary power, turn coordinator supporting bank, heading indicator primary bank, VSI supporting pitch. No instrument is labeled primary pitch.

f3.caption: Figure 7-26. Stabilized climb at constant airspeed.
f3.alt: Six-pack panel in a steady climb: airspeed indicator labeled primary pitch, attitude indicator supporting pitch and bank, heading indicator primary bank, turn coordinator supporting bank, VSI supporting pitch.

f4.caption: Figure 7-33. Standard rate turn, constant airspeed.
f4.alt: Six-pack panel in a left turn. Labels: airspeed indicator primary power, attitude indicator primary bank initially and supporting pitch, altimeter primary pitch, turn coordinator primary bank as the turn is established, heading indicator primary bank, VSI supporting pitch.

f5.caption: Figure 7-29. Level off at cruising speed.
f5.alt: Six-pack panel at the level-off: altimeter labeled primary pitch, attitude indicator supporting pitch and bank, airspeed indicator primary power as airspeed approaches the desired value, heading indicator primary bank, turn coordinator supporting bank, VSI supporting pitch.

f6.caption: Figure 7-63. Constant airspeed climb from cruise airspeed.
f6.alt: Primary flight display. A small inset shows level flight at 5,000 feet, 120 knots, 23 inches and 2300 RPM. The main display shows the yellow chevron raised, 25 inches and 2500 RPM labeled primary power, a 500 fpm trend at 5,040 feet with a primary pitch label pointing at the altitude tape, and the heading indicator labeled primary bank.

f7.caption: Figure 6-17. Radial cross-check.
f7.alt: Instrument panel with yellow arrows pointing outward from the attitude indicator toward the airspeed indicator, altimeter, turn coordinator, heading indicator and vertical speed indicator, showing the eyes moving out from and back to the attitude indicator. Manifold pressure and RPM gauges are at the right.

scenario.title: Hood climbs on a hazy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are teaching a private pilot learner with about 2 hours of hood time in a fixed-pitch trainer. The practice area is busy with training traffic, the haze is thickening, and the learner came straight from a long workday. Today's plan: constant airspeed climbs from 3,500 to 5,500 feet, straight and with standard-rate turns, under a view-limiting device.

questions.q: What do you brief about the airplane and the plan before the device goes on?
questions.a: This trainer's climb speed and climb power from the POH/AFM [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], the climb picture in bar widths, that RPM falls in a long climb with a fixed-pitch propeller so the throttle must come forward [[24:80|AFH 3-19]], the 10 percent lead [[23:177|IFH 7-16]], and when and how the device goes on and comes off (FAA-S-ACS-25, Equipment Requirements & Limitations).

questions.q: On the first entry the nose goes up about three bar widths and the VSI jumps around. What do you say?
questions.a: That is overcontrolling pitch on entry; make small pressures and wait for the result [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. An abrupt pitch change makes the VSI erratic and can even reverse it, so do not chase it [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

questions.q: In the climbing turn the bank stays right on standard rate, but the airspeed bleeds 12 knots. What is the fault and the fix?
questions.a: Preoccupation with bank: the pitch instruments were not checked as the bank went in [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Check pitch as the bank pressure starts, and hold the climb airspeed with pitch, since the airspeed is the pitch reference in the climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

questions.q: Halfway up, you notice the suction gauge is below its green arc. What now?
questions.a: The attitude and heading indicators may be unreliable when suction is low [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Take the controls or remove the hood if needed, cross-check the turn coordinator, airspeed, altimeter and VSI, and treat it as a deteriorating situation; be ready to take over [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

questions.q: When the hood comes off, the haze has closed in and you have no horizon. What do you do?
questions.a: Without a horizon you are in IMC for practical purposes [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]; you are already in an urgency condition, so ask ATC for help now [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Fly the instruments, avoid combined maneuvers [[24:370|AFH 18-21]], and consider a precautionary landing early [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

questions.q: Over the last 20 minutes the learner's timing has gone off and they fixate more. What is happening, and what do you do?
questions.a: Skill fatigue: timing disruption and attention narrowing to the center of vision [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. End the hood work; fixation is also a sign that tasks need more practice in isolation next lesson [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

skills.do: From the right seat, demonstrate and explain the transition from cruise to the climb pitch attitude and climb power on an assigned heading, saying which instruments you are using, how you coordinate rudder with the power change and when you trim. The ACS text: "Transition to the climb pitch attitude and power setting on an assigned heading using proper instrument cross-check and interpretation, and coordinated flight control application." (ACS AI.XI.B.S1)
skills.practice: With a safety pilot, fly entries from cruise and from climb speed while talking: pitch picture in bar widths, power, right rudder, trim [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

skills.do: Climb at a constant airspeed to altitudes the examiner assigns, straight and in standard-rate turns, explaining the primary instruments and the bank you are using. The ACS text: "Climb at a constant airspeed to specific altitudes in straight flight and turns." (ACS AI.XI.B.S2)
skills.practice: Practice climbing turns both ways at standard rate, using 15 percent of true airspeed for bank and the turn coordinator to confirm it [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

skills.do: Level off at the assigned altitude and hold it while explaining the lead and the power change. The ACS text: "Level off at the assigned altitude and maintain altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, and airspeed ±10 knots." (ACS AI.XI.B.S3)
skills.practice: Call the lead aloud (10 percent of the VSI) and practice level-offs both at cruise and at climb airspeed [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

skills.do: The examiner, playing your learner, makes a climb error such as chasing the VSI, an overcontrolled entry, no trim or no level-off lead. Name it, explain the cause, demonstrate the fix, and coach a retry. The ACS text: "Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task." (ACS AI.XI.B.S4)
skills.practice: For each row of the error table, practice "what I see, why, the fix" in one breath, then fly the fix [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

quiz.q: In the IFH climb entry figure (7-25), which instrument is labeled primary for bank?
options: The attitude indicator
The turn coordinator
The heading indicator
The vertical speed indicator
quiz.why: During the climb entry the heading indicator is primary for bank; the attitude indicator and turn coordinator support [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: What does the CFI ACS require after the level-off in this Task?
options: Altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots
Altitude ±200 feet, heading ±20°, airspeed ±10 knots
Altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, and airspeed ±5 knots
Altitude ±150 feet, heading ±15°, airspeed ±10 knots
quiz.why: ACS AI.XI.B.S3. The ±200 feet and ±20° figures are the Private ACS (PA.VIII.B.S3).

quiz.q: On the IFH analog climb-entry figure (7-25), which instrument is labeled primary for pitch?
options: None; the figure labels only supporting pitch
The airspeed indicator, as in the stabilized climb
The altimeter, as in the PFD entry figure
The vertical speed indicator, as in a constant-rate climb
quiz.why: Figure 7-25 labels the attitude indicator and VSI as supporting pitch and gives no primary pitch label; the airspeed becomes primary once the climb is stable [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The PFD entry figure (7-63) points primary pitch at the altitude readout [[23:207|IFH 7-46]].

quiz.q: In a standard-rate climbing turn at 120 knots true airspeed, the turn coordinator sits on the standard-rate mark, but the attitude indicator shows 16° of bank, not the 18° of the rule of thumb. What do you teach?
options: Steepen to 18°, since the rule of thumb sets the bank for standard rate
Keep the turn coordinator on the mark and note the exact bank it takes there
Suspect the turn coordinator, since the two should agree exactly
Add power until the bank and the turn rate agree with the rule
quiz.why: The rule of thumb is approximate. Roll in on the attitude indicator, then hold the turn coordinator on the standard-rate mark as primary for bank and note the exact bank it takes [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; the bank for standard rate varies slightly [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

quiz.q: The IFH has no primary and supporting figure for a climbing turn. What does its text tell you to do?
options: Fly the level-turn figure (7-33) as drawn, altimeter primary for pitch
Hold the straight-climb VSI rate with pitch all the way through the turn
Avoid climbing turns under the hood until the learner is instrument rated
Combine the climb and turn techniques and speed up the cross-check
quiz.why: Combine the straight-climb technique with the turn techniques, allow for lift and power, and increase the cross-check to cover bank as well as pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Figure 7-33 is a level turn [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; avoiding combined maneuvers is AFH advice for untrained pilots in IMC [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

quiz.q: Your learner takes about 5 seconds to roll into a climbing turn and watches only the bank instruments while she does. What does the IFH say to do instead?
options: Finish the roll-in, then check the pitch and power instruments together
Roll in faster, so the pitch has less time to wander
Check the pitch instruments as soon as the bank pressure starts
Keep the heading indicator in the scan until the bank is set
quiz.why: Preoccupation with bank on entry is a listed pitch error: if 5 seconds are needed to roll in, check the pitch instruments as the bank pressures start and control the total attitude, not one factor at a time [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

quiz.q: In the stable climb your learner moves the attitude indicator's miniature aircraft down onto the horizon bar "so the picture looks level." What does the IFH say?
options: Fine, as long as it is reset to cruise after the level-off
Leave it set for level cruise so it shows the true pitch in the climb
Required, because the climb picture must read level to trim well
Fine on an electric gyro, but never on a vacuum-driven one
quiz.why: Set the miniature aircraft at cruise in level flight; otherwise do not change it for flight at other speeds, so the attitude indicator shows a true pitch picture in all maneuvers [[23:138|IFH 6-5]].

quiz.q: Per the IFH electronic display section, what is the airplane actually trimmed for?
options: A pitch attitude on the display
A power setting on the gauge
An airspeed
An altitude
quiz.why: A listed trim error is not understanding that the aircraft is trimmed for airspeed, not a pitch attitude [[23:206|IFH 7-45]].

quiz.q: In any instrument maneuver the IFH says to attend to the most important tasks first. What does it say to keep relatively constant, so more time is free for cross-check and interpretation?
options: The pitch attitude
The power setting on the gauge
The bank angle
The trim wheel position
quiz.why: Attend to the most important tasks first; keep the pitch attitude relatively constant, and more time can be devoted to cross-check and instrument interpretation [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

quiz.q: In the IFH "climbing while accelerating" disorientation demonstration, what does the instructor actually do with the airplane?
options: Raises the nose slowly while holding the airspeed constant
Climbs at a constant airspeed in a shallow coordinated turn
Adds full power and lets the nose rise on its own
Accelerates while holding a straight-and-level attitude
quiz.why: With the pilot's eyes closed, the instructor holds approach airspeed straight and level, then accelerates while staying straight and level; the usual illusion is a climb [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

final_quiz.q: You cover the attitude indicator to simulate a vacuum failure, and your learner must climb 1,000 feet. How does the IFH suggest she enter the climb?
options: From cruise, raising the nose first and adding power as the speed nears climb speed
Slow to climb speed in level flight, then add climb power as the pitch comes up
Hold cruise airspeed with pitch and add full power, letting the VSI show the climb
Raise the nose one bar width, add power, and accept whatever airspeed results
final_quiz.why: Climb entries on partial panel are more easily and accurately controlled from climbing speed: slow in level flight first, then raise the pitch and add climb power together [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Without the attitude indicator there are no bar widths to set.

final_quiz.q: Playing your learner, the examiner climbs holding exactly 500 fpm on the VSI at climb power while the airspeed bleeds 12 knots below climb speed. What is the error?
options: Too little power: raise it until the VSI and airspeed both match the plan
None yet: the airspeed will recover once the VSI lag has passed
Trimmed for the rate: retrim for the climb picture and the speed follows
Flying constant rate: in this Task pitch holds the airspeed, not the VSI
final_quiz.why: In a constant airspeed climb the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch once stable and the rate settles where it settles; the VSI is primary for pitch only in a constant-rate climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Learners who know only the VSI tend to chase it [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing at 900 fpm to an assigned 6,000 feet, your learner starts the level-off at 5,980 and stops at 6,130. How does that compare with the standards, and what lead was due?
options: Inside both limits; a 20-foot lead is about right at that climb rate
Outside both limits; the lead should have been about 180 feet
Inside the CFI limit; a lead of about 9 feet would have worked
Outside the CFI limit but inside the private one; lead about 90 feet
final_quiz.why: 130 feet high is outside ±100 feet (ACS AI.XI.B.S3) but inside ±200 feet (PA.VIII.B.S3). Lead = 900 x 0.10 = 90 feet, so start at 5,910 feet [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: On a PFD, your learner raises the chevron to the planned climb pitch from cruise. Fifteen seconds later the airspeed tape is still slowly decreasing toward climb speed. What does it mean?
options: The pitch is too high: lower the chevron until the tape stops moving
Power is too low: add power until the tape stops moving
Normal: with the right pitch the speed slowly settles on the target
The trim is wrong: retrim nose-down now and let the speed recover
final_quiz.why: If the pitch attitude is correct, the airspeed should slowly decrease to the desired speed; if it varies, make small pitch changes, and any airspeed change needs a trim adjustment [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner shoves the throttle to climb power in one quick motion, and the heading swings 10° left before she reacts. What is the error and the fix?
options: Abrupt throttle: smooth power, right rudder, and a faster scan
A precessing heading indicator: reset it to the compass later
Normal at climb power: fix the heading once the climb has stabilized
Too much right rudder: ease off the rudder as the power comes in
final_quiz.why: Abrupt use of the throttle is a listed power error [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]. More power makes a single-engine airplane yaw and roll left unless aileron and rudder are applied, so the cross-check must speed up [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner moves from a 180 hp trainer to a 100 hp trainer and sets the same climb picture with full power. What should she expect?
options: The same airspeed and rate, since the attitude sets the performance
A different speed and rate; she must learn this airplane's picture
The same rate at a lower airspeed, since the picture fixes the rate
The same airspeed at a lower rate, since the picture fixes the speed
final_quiz.why: Attitude plus power gives performance: the same picture gives very different results in different airplanes [[23:146|IFH 6-13]], and the climb attitude varies with the type of airplane [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

final_quiz.q: A VFR-only pilot you trained is squeezed between a lowering ceiling and rising terrain, with an hour of fuel and the engine running fine. Per the AFH, which choice is generally less hazardous?
options: A climb into the clouds on instruments, asking for help once on top
Pressing on low under the ceiling, since the terrain may improve later
Waiting for engine trouble, so a forced landing is clearly justified
A precautionary landing now, with power and time to pick terrain
final_quiz.why: A precautionary landing is generally less hazardous than a forced one: more time to select terrain and plan, and power to fix errors. A non-instrument-rated pilot trapped by weather who does not consider one accepts an extremely hazardous alternative [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies solid straight climbs, but her climbing turns fall apart when you ask her to read the OAT. Per the AIH, what is the best next step?
options: Keep adding tasks until she copes, since overload is the fastest teacher
Practice the climbing turn alone until it is solid, then add the tasks back
Skip climbing turns and move on to unusual attitude recoveries
Give the extra tasks only on the ground, never in the airplane
final_quiz.why: Before combining tasks, make sure each can be done reasonably well in isolation; fixation on a task is often a sign it has not had enough practice alone [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

final_quiz.q: Playing your learner, the examiner levels off planning to stay at 90 knots, but the airspeed decays 8 knots below at the new altitude. What happened?
options: Power came off faster than the pitch came down; reduce power in proportion
Too little forward pressure, so the airplane kept climbing
The level-off lead was too large for the climb rate
The airspeed indicator lags during level-offs
final_quiz.why: To level off at climb airspeed, reduce power in proportion to the pitch change and the airspeed stays constant [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Poor pitch and power coordination on slow-speed level-offs is a listed error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

final_quiz.q: After 50 minutes of hood work at the end of the learner's workday, their timing gets slightly off and they stare at the center of the panel. What is this most likely?
options: Coriolis illusion from head movement
The leans after a long turn
Hypoxia from the climbs
Skill fatigue
final_quiz.why: Skill fatigue brings timing disruption and attention narrowing to the center of vision, with loss of smooth control [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing under the hood, ATC calls traffic at 12 o'clock, 2 miles, altitude unknown, and the nose blocks your view ahead. What is your best move?
options: Have the learner keep climbing so the traffic passes below you
Have the learner level off on instruments while you watch the panel
Lower the nose briefly, or have her do it, and scan ahead
Ask ATC for a vector and hold the climb attitude until they reply
final_quiz.why: In a climb, pilots can adjust the pitch attitude to improve the view over the nose [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]; see-and-avoid applies to every pilot whenever weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. Under the hood that scan is yours (application).

final_quiz.q: Your trainer powers the attitude and heading indicators by vacuum but the turn coordinator electrically. Why does the PHAK say aircraft are set up this way?
options: Because an electric gyro cannot show any pitch information
Because a vacuum gyro cannot sense a rate of turn at all
So bank information remains if one power source fails
Because the rules forbid vacuum power for rate instruments
final_quiz.why: Most aircraft have at least two sources of power so that at least one source of bank information is available if one power source fails [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

final_quiz.q: Partway up, the suction gauge reads below its normal range. What should the learner conclude?
options: Only the turn coordinator is affected
The attitude and heading indicators may be unreliable
The airspeed indicator will read low
Nothing changes until the gauge reads zero
final_quiz.why: Attitude and heading indicators may not give reliable information when suction is low; gyros may become unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

takeaways: Entry: attitude first on the attitude indicator, climb power with it or right after, right rudder, then trim [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
Stable climb: airspeed is primary for pitch, heading indicator for bank, tachometer or manifold pressure for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

Climbing turns: straight-climb technique plus turn technique, with a faster cross-check [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. From the turn technique, the turn coordinator is primary for bank at standard rate [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; pitch still holds the climb airspeed.
Level off with a 10 percent lead; to cruise, keep climb power until the speed nears cruise [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].
Fixation and omission show in the eyes: watch them, and practice tasks in isolation first [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].
Under the hood, the outside scan is yours: do not look inside too long [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].
cfi_notes: IFH 6-5 says the miniature aircraft is set at cruise and should not be changed for flight at other speeds [[23:138|IFH 6-5]], while IFH 5-19 describes the knob as compensating for pitch trim changes as airspeed changes [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. Teach 6-5: set it at cruise and leave it, so the climb picture stays consistent.

Primary pitch labels: Figure 7-25 (analog entry) labels no primary pitch instrument, Figure 7-63 (PFD entry) points a primary pitch label at the altitude readout, and the text names no primary pitch for the entry and makes the airspeed primary once stable [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:207|IFH 7-46]] [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]. Teach the text and explain the labels if a learner asks.

The IFH lets power go in with the pitch change or after it from cruise [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]; the AFH visual climb adds them together [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Pick one entry and teach it the same way visually and under the hood.
The AFH emergency climb (no more than one bar width, accept the speed) is not the ACS constant airspeed climb [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Learners mix them up; name the one you are flying.

The IFH has no primary and supporting figure for a climbing turn. Figure 7-33 is a level turn with the altimeter primary for pitch and the airspeed primary for power [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Only its bank roles carry over; holding the climb airspeed with pitch in the turn is your application of the IFH advice to combine the two techniques [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].
Your learners are tested to ±200 feet and ±20° (PA.VIII.B.S3); you are tested to ±100 feet and ±10° (AI.XI.B.S3). Fly your demonstrations to the tighter numbers.

The IFH straight-and-level error list still mentions uncaging the attitude indicator [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]; many newer instruments have no caging mechanism [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. Teach it only if your trainer has one.
Fig 7-25 and 7-26 show a constant-speed propeller panel. With a fixed-pitch propeller the tachometer is the power instrument, and RPM falls in a long climb [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
gaps: Climb airspeed, climb power and the climb pitch picture in bar widths are airplane-specific: POH/AFM and in-flight calibration.
No source gives a level-off lead for a climbing turn that rolls out and levels off at the same time; use the 10 percent and half-bank leads separately.
The sources give no maximum length for a hood session before fatigue sets in; judge the learner (PHAK 17-13 lists the signs).
The ACS asks the applicant to provide a view-limiting device but does not name a type; the instructor and examiner brief its use.
No source gives a standard pitch picture for a climbing turn; the attitude indicator picture changes with bank and airplane.

pins.label: Primary for pitch in the stable climb
Primary for pitch during the level-off
Primary for bank once a standard-rate turn is established
Primary for bank in the straight climb

activities.title: Read the panel
activities.intro: Tap what the panel shows, then the best interpretation.

pairs.l: Hot, heavy day: airspeed on target, VSI lower than usual
pairs.r: Normal; weight and air density change the rate

pairs.l: Airspeed eases off for a few seconds after a smooth pitch-up
pairs.r: The airplane slowing, not instrument lag

pairs.l: Heading drifting left just after adding power
pairs.r: Left yaw from power: rudder and aileron

pairs.l: Wings level on the attitude indicator, ball off center
pairs.r: Skidding: center the ball with rudder

pairs.l: Altimeter frozen and VSI on zero at climb power
Heading indicator 10° off the compass after a long climb

activities.title: Instrument climb numbers
activities.intro: Work each one out, then type your answer.

items.q: Climbing from 3,500 to 5,500 feet at a steady 500 fpm, how many minutes after the climb starts do you reach the level-off lead point?
A standard-rate climbing turn from heading 090° to 270° at a steady 500 fpm. About how many feet does the airplane gain during the turn?
items.why: Standard rate is 3° per second [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]: 180 ÷ 3 = 60 seconds = 1 minute; 1 x 500 = 500 feet. In practice the climb is a little shallower in a bank at fixed power [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

items.q: Your learner climbs at 750 fpm and starts the level-off 30 feet before the altitude. How many feet later than the IFH lead did she start?
After a smooth pitch-up, your learner checks the VSI 2 seconds later. Using the PHAK lag, at least how many more seconds before the needle shows a stable rate?
items.why: The needle stabilizes after about 6 to 9 seconds [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]: 6 - 2 = 4 seconds at least.

activities.title: What the panel does at a level-off to cruise
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Reach the lead point, 10 percent of the vertical speed below the altitude
Smooth, steady forward pressure toward the level attitude for cruise
VSI moves slowly toward zero and the altimeter slows
Airspeed builds with climb power still set
Reduce to cruise power as the airspeed approaches cruise
Trim off the pressures and resume the straight-and-level cross-check

activities.title: Fixation, omission or emphasis?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap the fault it shows.

items.t: Watches the airspeed needle through the whole entry while the heading drifts
Stares at the tachometer while setting climb power, waiting for the speed to change
Never rechecks the heading indicator after adding power, not expecting it to move
Skips the tachometer for the whole long climb, so falling RPM goes unseen
Holds the climb by the attitude indicator alone because it is the easiest to read
Sets climb pitch by the VSI alone because it is the instrument she knows best

activities.title: True or false: hazards in instrument climbs
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Uncoordinated turns, especially climbing turns, can send misleading signals to the inner ear.
cards.why: True. Uncoordinated turns, especially climbing turns, can send misleading signals to the brain [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

cards.s: In unplanned IMC, flying partly by the instruments while searching outside for visual confirmation is a safe way to ease in.
cards.why: False. Splitting attention that way results in inadequate airplane control and may lead to spatial disorientation and loss of control [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

cards.s: A pilot unable to hold attitude by the natural horizon is in IMC for practical purposes, whatever the reported weather.
Untrained instrument pilots should use climbing turns to save time when ATC is busy.
cards.why: False. Combined maneuvers should be avoided if at all possible by an untrained instrument pilot [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

cards.s: Stress beyond a pilot's ability to cope makes performance fall off sharply.
cards.why: True. Stress that exceeds the ability to cope causes performance to fall sharply [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

cards.s: Hood training for the private certificate prepares a pilot to fly in instrument meteorological conditions.
cards.why: False. Learners must understand that this introduction to the instruments does not prepare them for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

activities.title: First instrument climb lesson
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your learner flies steady straight-and-level under the hood. Today: constant airspeed climbs. The lesson unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: Before the first hood climb, which instrument skill should the learner already fly well?
options: Steep turns under the hood, since climbs are easier than those
Airspeed changes in straight-and-level flight on instruments
Unusual attitude recoveries, so she can save a climb that goes bad
Partial-panel turns, since the climb uses the same scan
steps.why: Airspeed changes in straight-and-level flight build all three basic instrument skills [[23:172|IFH 7-11]], and the entry from climb speed starts with that same speed reduction [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

steps.s: Which entry do you teach first?
options: From cruise with a climbing turn, to save time
From climb speed, straight ahead, after slowing in level flight
From cruise on partial panel, to build confidence
Whichever the learner picks
steps.why: The IFH has the airspeed reduction done first in level flight, so the entry then changes only pitch and power together [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. It also says partial-panel entries are easier from climb speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

steps.s: In the straight climb the airspeed is on target, but the ball sits right of center and the learner holds right aileron to keep the wings level. Your coaching?
options: More right aileron, since the left wing keeps dropping
Right rudder to center the ball, then trim off the pressure
Left rudder, since the nose is yawing to the left
Nothing; a small slip is normal at climb power
steps.why: More power makes the airplane yaw and roll left unless aileron and rudder are applied [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Step on the ball: right rudder centers it [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]], then trim off the pressure [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

steps.s: Rolling out of the climbing turn on the assigned heading, the learner keeps all the back pressure she held in the bank, and the airspeed starts to drop. What do you say?
options: Hold it; the speed comes back once the wings are level
Add power above climb power to keep the speed up
Ease the back pressure as the wings level, back to the climb picture
Roll back into the bank until the airspeed recovers
steps.why: As the bank comes out the vertical lift component increases; not adjusting pitch on the roll-out is a listed turn error [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. In the climb, pitch holds the airspeed at fixed climb power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] (application).
